in_context.text: Paul has just asked Philemon to take Onesimus back "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (1:16). Now he builds on his own friendship with Philemon: if Philemon counts Paul a partner, he should welcome Onesimus the way he would welcome Paul himself. In the next verses Paul even offers to pay whatever Onesimus owes (1:18-19).

speaker.text: Paul, writing from prison with Timothy (1:1, 1:9).

audience.text: Philemon, Paul's "dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer," in whose house a church met (1:1-2).

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant who had left him and had become a believer through Paul (1:10-11, 1:15).

what.text: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "as myself." He links the welcome Philemon gives Onesimus to the partnership Philemon shares with Paul.

events.text: Onesimus had "departed" from Philemon for a season and was now being sent back by Paul (1:12, 1:15).

written.text: Traditional: about AD 60-62, during Paul's imprisonment in Rome. Scholarly: nearly all accept Paul wrote it; some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul writes from prison; the letter does not name the city, and Rome is the traditional view. It went to Philemon's household, traditionally linked to Colossae (Colossians 4:9, 4:17).

purpose.text: Paul appeals for love's sake rather than giving an order (1:8-9). He wants Philemon's welcome of Onesimus to be willing, not forced (1:14).

big_picture.text: Paul makes the same request as in 1:12, "receive him." Jesus taught that receiving one he sends is receiving him (Matthew 10:40). Here Paul stands in for Onesimus, so a welcome given to the one counts as given to the other.

for_readers.text: Fellowship with other believers is meant to show itself in how we receive those they love, even one who was once "unprofitable" (1:11).

why_it_matters.text: The word means a partner, associate or companion, and also a sharer. Paul uses it of Titus, "my partner and fellowhelper" (2 Corinthians 8:23). Paul's appeal rests on this shared bond with Philemon.
It means to take to oneself or receive, used of persons. The same verb appears in Romans 14:1 and 15:7, so Paul is asking Philemon to take Onesimus in, not just to let him back.
This is a conditional particle that can state a general assumption. Paul builds his request on something he assumes is true: that Philemon does count him a partner.

takeaway.text: Paul puts himself in Onesimus's place. If Philemon values his partnership with Paul, he should welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul.

resolved.reason: Matthew 18:5 speaks of receiving a little child in Jesus' name, not of receiving "one he sends." Citing it for that teaching misrepresents the verse.

resolved.reason: Verse 1:18 is conditional ("If he hath wronged thee"), and 1:11 says only that Onesimus was "unprofitable." Neither verse states that Onesimus actually wronged Philemon, so "someone who once did us wrong" overstates the sources.
